title: $20 an Hour Is How Much a Year? (2026)
metaDescription: $20/hour is $41,600 a year at 40 hrs/week — $3,467 monthly, $1,600.00 biweekly. See overtime pay tables and a 2026 federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Full time at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, overtime tables at time-and-a-half, and a 2026 federal-only take-home estimate.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $20 an hour per year?
shortAnswer.html: $20 an hour is $41,600 a year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). That's $800.00 a week, $1,600.00 biweekly, and $3,466.67 a month gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $35,606 — and steady overtime at $30.00/hour raises the total fast.

sections.title: What $20/hour adds up to per period.
sections.note: Gross (pre-tax) figures assuming paid hours every week of the year. Unpaid time off reduces them proportionally.

sections.title: $20 an hour in 2026, in plain numbers.
paragraphs: A $20/hour wage annualizes to $41,600 at full time ($20 × 2,080 hours). Hourly workers rarely see exactly that: unpaid days off pull it down, while overtime — paid at time-and-a-half — pushes it up fast.

That annual figure lands about 36% below the U.S. median full-time wage: BLS median weekly earnings are $1,251 (BLS, Q2 2026), which is roughly $31.28 an hour at 40 hours. Unlike most salaried roles, hourly jobs are usually overtime-eligible — see the table below for what that's worth.

sections.title: Overtime at $30.00/hour changes the math quickly.
sections.note: Overtime rows assume time-and-a-half (1.5 × $20 = $30.00) on hours past 40, every week of the year — the FLSA baseline for non-exempt workers.

sections.title: From $41,600 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, credits, or pre-tax benefits. Actual checks vary.

sections.title: What a single filer actually keeps.
paragraphs: After the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100, a single filer earning $41,600 owes about $2,812 in federal income tax (effective rate 6.8%, marginal bracket 12%) and $3,182 in Social Security and Medicare. That leaves roughly $35,606 — about $1,369.45 per biweekly check — before any state income tax.

faq.q: How much is $20 an hour per year?
faq.a: $20 an hour is $41,600 a year at full time — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). At 30 hours a week it comes to $31,200, and with 10 hours of weekly overtime it reaches about $57,200.

faq.q: How much is $20 an hour biweekly?
faq.a: A standard 80-hour biweekly period at $20/hour grosses $1,600.00. After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $1,369.45 remains per check, before state taxes.

faq.q: How much is $20 an hour after taxes?
faq.a: On $41,600 of annual wages, a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction pays about $2,812 of federal income tax plus $3,182 of FICA, keeping roughly $35,606 a year — about $17.12 per hour worked. State and local taxes reduce this further where they apply.

faq.q: How much is $20 an hour with overtime?
faq.a: Overtime pays time-and-a-half: $30.00 per hour past 40 in a week. A steady 50-hour week earns $1,100.00 weekly — $57,200 a year, $15,600 more than the straight 40-hour year.

faq.q: Is $20 an hour a good wage in 2026?
faq.a: $20/hour annualizes to $41,600, which is about 36% below the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median for full-time workers is $1,251/week (about $31.28/hour, BLS, Q2 2026). Local cost of living, benefits, and schedule stability matter as much as the rate itself.

methodology: Annualization is straight arithmetic: $20 × 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks) = $41,600, with daily/weekly/biweekly/monthly rows derived the same way. No unpaid leave is assumed.
Overtime rows use the FLSA non-exempt baseline of 1.5× base pay ($30.00/hour) on hours over 40 per week, sustained all 52 weeks.
The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction plus employee FICA (7.65%). It excludes state/local tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits.
Median-wage comparison: BLS median usual weekly earnings, full-time workers, $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
Educational estimates only — not tax, legal, or financial advice.
